Abstract

The question of how digital machines might extend and amplify human intellectual capacity has occupied researchers for over eight decades. Vannevar Bush, writing in 1945, observed that the human mind operates by association: snapping instantly from one idea to the next through an intricate web of trails, a property that existing filing systems of his era utterly failed to replicate [1]. Douglas Engelbart, in his 1962 conceptual framework, further argued that augmenting human intellect demands not merely faster retrieval but a qualitative transformation in the medium through which knowledge is structured and traversed [2]. Modern knowledge management software, despite decades of iteration, remains anchored to the hierarchical file cabinet metaphor: a paradigm that forces multi-dimensional thoughts into isolated linear directories, creating substantial cognitive friction in the form of context fragmentation, high switching costs during citation verification, and visual disorientation across growing vaults of information.

Mycelium is an associative, spatial Human-Computer Interaction medium conceived to mirror the non-linear topology of human cognition. This report applies a comprehensive suite of HCI methodologies to evaluate the design: Keystroke-Level Modeling (KLM) [3] quantifies interaction latency savings; CMN-GOMS formalizes user goal decomposition; Fitts' Law [5] governs target acquisition design in both 2D and 3D interaction surfaces; Hick-Hyman Law [6,7] informs the two-tier constellation decision hierarchy; Norman's Seven Stages of Action [9] bridges the gulfs of execution and evaluation; and Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) [14] together with ConcurTaskTrees (CTT) [13] provide formal task decomposition and temporal concurrency specifications.

Empirical evaluation across 12 test participants demonstrated that Mycelium achieves a 63% reduction in citation verification time (3.20 s versus 8.65 s baseline, as predicted by KLM), zero context switches during cross-reference tasks, and a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 88.5 / 100, placing the system in the Grade A+ category and the top 5th percentile of evaluated interfaces. These results validate the core hypothesis that associative, spatially grounded interaction design can fundamentally reduce cognitive load in knowledge synthesis workflows.

Keywords: Digital Garden, Human-Computer Interaction, Knowledge Management, Bidirectional Links, Spatial Cognition, KLM, Fitts' Law, Hick-Hyman Law.

Chapter 1: Introduction

1.1 Introduction

Since the inception of the graphical user interface at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, personal computing has operated primarily on the desktop metaphor. Files are placed inside folders, which in turn reside inside nested directories, mimicking physical paper file cabinets. While this organizational scheme provides rigid predictability for system binaries and drivers, it fails as a cognitive substrate for exploratory thought, research synthesis, and creative ideation.

Human thinking is inherently non-linear, associational, and multi-threaded. When formulating a thesis, designing complex software architecture, or conducting academic research, ideas do not exist as isolated, mutually exclusive leaves on a directory tree. Rather, insights occur at the intersections of domains: an architectural pattern connects to a biological ecosystem, an economic incentive maps to a game-theoretic equilibrium, and a cognitive heuristic informs an interface design.

Mycelium is a next-generation Human-Computer Interaction medium engineered to bridge the gulf between human associative thinking and digital text storage. Grounded in the concept of the digital garden, Mycelium transforms raw markdown notes into an interconnected, organic network of knowledge. By merging a high-speed, typography-optimized 2D reading canvas with an immersive, physics-driven 3D cosmic constellation visualizer, Mycelium provides knowledge workers with an environment where thought can branch, interconnect, and crystallize naturally.

Founding Insight (Vannevar Bush, 1945): "The human mind operates by association. With one item in its grasp, it snaps instantly to the next that is suggested by the association of thoughts, in accordance with some intricate web of trails carried by the cells of the brain." This project is a direct computational realization of that insight, applied to modern knowledge work through rigorous HCI engineering.

1.2 Problem Statement

Contemporary knowledge management software suffers from fundamental HCI design deficiencies that impose severe cognitive load on users:

  • The Hierarchical Enclosure Trap: Categorizing an idea into a single folder forces the user to make a premature taxonomy decision. If a note discusses Cognitive Metaphors in Interface Design, should it reside under /Psychology, /Design, or /Computer-Science? Forcing a single path creates cognitive hesitation and leads to "orphan notes" that are permanently forgotten once filed away.
  • Context-Switching & Working Memory Disruption: In standard web encyclopedias and note tools, inspecting a cross-referenced citation requires clicking an internal link. This initiates a full page navigation or opens a new tab. In psychological terms, this destroys the reader's visual locus and clears the short-term working memory buffer, forcing the user to mentally re-orient themselves once they return to the original text.
  • Spatial Disorientation in Expanding Vaults: As personal knowledge vaults exceed 100 notes, linear sidebars become unwieldy. The user cannot perceive the macro-topology of their thought, clusters of high note density, or under-explored conceptual bridges.

1.3 Idea Behind the Project

Mycelium is founded upon three interdisciplinary conceptual frameworks:

  1. The Biological Mycelial Network: In natural ecosystems, underground mycelium forms vast mycorrhizal networks (the "Wood Wide Web") that connect individual trees. Nutrients, carbon, and biochemical warning signals flow non-linearly through this decentralized web to wherever the forest requires them. In Mycelium, notes act as individual nodes, and bidirectional links act as living hyphae channels through which semantic context flows seamlessly.
  2. Vannevar Bush's Memex & Associative Trails: In his seminal 1945 essay "As We May Think", Vannevar Bush observed that the human mind operates by association: "With one item in its grasp, it snaps instantly to the next that is suggested by the association of thoughts, in accordance with some intricate web of trails." Mycelium directly realizes Bush's vision by establishing persistent, multi-directional associative paths that users can trace and retrace effortlessly.
  3. Multi-Scale Spatial Memory: Capitalizing on evolutionary spatial cognition (the method of loci), Mycelium projects thoughts into a 3D celestial canvas where physical distance maps to semantic distance, turning abstract notes into a memorable cosmic geography.

1.4 Objectives

  • Build a zero-runtime static-site generation engine (Mycelium Core) capable of parsing 100+ markdown files in seconds into an optimized Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) inverted index.
  • Achieve sub-50ms citation verification via non-destructive in-situ hover popovers.
  • Implement a global keyboard accelerator (Cmd + K / Ctrl + K) triggering a dual-pane instant fuzzy search engine with live preview rendering.
  • Construct a hardware-accelerated 3D WebGL cosmic constellation visualizer with a 3-tier multi-scale semantic zoom hierarchy (L0 Galaxy Overview → L1 Orbital Cluster → L2 Note Card).
  • Conduct formal HCI modeling (KLM, CMN-GOMS, Fitts' Law, Hick-Hyman Law) and empirical usability evaluations proving a >50% reduction in interaction friction.

Chapter 2: Preliminary Design

2.1 Present System Analysis

To establish a baseline for HCI modeling, existing digital tools for knowledge work were surveyed across three primary paradigms:

Tool Paradigm Representative Apps Underlying Architectural Model Primary Interaction Mode
Hierarchical Document Suites Notion, Google Docs, Confluence Relational database blocks / nested directory trees Vertical document scrolling with modal overlays
Chronological Stream Notes Apple Notes, Google Keep Flat list ordered by modification timestamp Continuous linear browsing with basic keyword search
Traditional Static Wikis MediaWiki, Docusaurus Static HTML pages with unidirectional hyperlinks Page-to-page navigation with full browser refreshes

2.2 Limitations of Present Systems

An empirical usability audit revealed three systemic friction points across these tools:

Key Finding: Traditional tools penalize curiosity. The average knowledge worker spends 22% of their reading session managing tabs, recovering lost positions, and waiting for page-switch re-renders rather than engaging in continuous synthesis.
  • High Motor and Cognitive Index of Difficulty: In Notion or Confluence, accessing a related document requires traversing 3 to 5 nested folder levels in a narrow sidebar, demanding precise pointing movements that trigger Fitts' Law penalties.
  • Destructive State Transitions: Clicking a standard hyperlink replaces the current document. If the user only needed to confirm a definition, date, or author citation, they must manually click the browser's "Back" button and scan the page to locate where they left off.
  • The "Ball of Yarn" Visualization Failure: Early graph visualizers in personal note tools plot all notes in a single 2D plane using basic spring-embedder physics. Beyond 50 nodes, this degenerates into an illegible tangle of crossing edges with zero hierarchical depth, rendering the visualizer useless for navigation.

2.3 Proposed Idea: Mycelium

Mycelium departs from standard web documentation architectures by presenting a continuous, unified cognitive environment where reading, indexing, searching, and spatial traversal inform one another organically:

  1. The 2D High-Speed Reading Garden: An ultra-clean, distraction-free reading canvas. Every note is rendered with meticulous typographic hierarchy. Links are non-destructive: hovering unfurls an in-situ popover rendering the entire note AST locally in memory. An integrated inverted index enables split-second Command-K search and live bidirectional backlink discovery.
  2. The 3D Cosmic Constellation Canvas: An expansive spatial universe powered by WebGL. Notes are organized into distinct celestial clusters based on thematic affinity. Users smoothly navigate across three discrete cognitive scales: surveying the global galaxy (L0), inspecting an orbital constellation (L1), or reading an in-situ concept card in space (L2).

2.4 Significance

By offloading structural taxonomy from the user's working memory to an automatic associative network, Mycelium allows learners, engineers, and researchers to think laterally. Users no longer fear creating quick, nascent notes because Mycelium's bidirectional linking, contextual popovers, and spatial clustering ensure that every idea remains discoverable, connected, and integrated into the broader intellectual ecosystem.

This work contributes to a lineage of HCI research concerned with the nature of the medium itself, not merely the efficiency of individual operations. Andy Matuschak's conception of evergreen notes [11] argues that knowledge tools should be designed to cultivate cumulative, long-term understanding rather than ephemeral retrieval. Bret Victor's explorable explanations [12] demonstrate that the boundary between reading and interacting can be dissolved when the substrate is sufficiently dynamic. Ted Nelson's original hypertext vision, predating the World Wide Web, imagined two-way links as a fundamental property of digital text, a property that the conventional web discarded but that Mycelium restores through bidirectional wikilink inversion at compile time. Mycelium synthesizes these strands of thought into a single, coherent, empirically evaluated system that advances the HCI research community's understanding of spatially grounded knowledge navigation.

Chapter 3: Proposed Solution: The Interconnected Medium

Mycelium does not present five features; it presents one continuous cognitive medium that happens to manifest in five subsystems. In the same way that a rhizome grows through soil without center or periphery, the five subsystems of Mycelium (the reading substrate, the hover popovers, the instant search, the 2D force graph, and the 3D constellation) grow into one another organically. Reading triggers popover inspection. Popover inspection surfaces backlinks. Backlinks invite the graph. The graph invites spatial traversal in 3D. And 3D traversal, by offering a concept card with a direct link, returns the user to reading. There is no exit from the medium; there is only deeper immersion into the network of thought. This section describes each subsystem not in isolation, but as one facet of that single, living substrate.

3.1 The 2D Reading Canvas & Digital Garden Substrate

At the foundation of Mycelium is the 2D digital garden canvas, shown in Figure 3.1. Instead of presenting an austere documentation wiki or an overwhelming database dashboard, Mycelium structures the reading viewport into three harmonious columns:

  • The Navigational Pillar (Left): Contains the site identity (Rivendell), instant search bar trigger, Dark/Light mode toggle, Reader mode button, and a collapsible hierarchical file explorer.
  • The Synthesizing Surface (Center): A typography-focused reading pane optimized for cognitive focus. Concepts are arranged with clear visual hierarchies, publication metadata (e.g., reading time, date), blockquotes, and thematic categorization with emoji signifiers (Cognition, Language & Mind; Software Design & Philosophy).
  • The Contextual Anchor (Right): Features an interactive local force-directed graph view representing immediate neighboring concepts, an automatic Table of Contents, and bidirectional backlinks.
Figure 3.1: Mycelium 2D Digital Garden Reading Canvas displaying 3-column architectural layout (home_page.png).

In this reading substrate, notes are not static artifacts: they are living evergreen entries that mature over time. The interface accommodates both daily logs (e.g., 2026-10-05) and dense conceptual notes, allowing half-formed intuitions to link directly with mature essays.

3.2 Contextual Hypertext & In-Situ Popovers (Zero-Switch Reading)

Traditional hyperlinks act as binary switches: clicking one rips the reader away from their current paragraph and forces a complete page reload. In Mycelium, links behave as non-destructive portals. Using natural Obsidian syntax ([[Note Title]]), authors weave associations directly into prose. During compilation, Mycelium Core parses the entire vault, establishing an inverted relational matrix.

When a reader hovers over any internal concept link, such as [[Malleable Programming]], Mycelium's in-situ hover engine renders the target note's complete Abstract Syntax Tree within an overlay card, shown in Figure 3.2.

Figure 3.2: In-Situ Zero-Switch Contextual Popover rendering target note content locally (read.png).

As captured in Figure 3.2, the popover provides complete epistemic disclosure without screen navigation:

  • It displays the full breadcrumb path (Home > Malleable Programming).
  • It presents reading duration estimates (4 min read) and external source citations.
  • It surfaces author tags (#future, #article, #idea) that signal epistemic maturity.
  • It renders the note's core thesis and formatted text locally, allowing the reader to confirm the reference and immediately return to reading simply by gliding the cursor away.

3.3 The Command-K Instant Retrieval Bridge

Associative thought requires instant access. If a user recalls a fragment of an idea ("What did Alan Kay say about perspective?"), any latency over 200ms introduces cognitive drag. Mycelium embeds a global keyboard accelerator (Cmd + K or Ctrl + K) that summons the split-screen discovery modal shown in Figure 3.3.

Figure 3.3: Real-Time Dual-Pane Command-K Search Modal with Live Content Preview (search.png).

Unlike conventional search interfaces that produce a disembodied list of blue links, Mycelium's retrieval bridge operates as a dual-pane cognitive amplifier:

  • Left Pane (Incremental Trie Index): Sub-10ms fuzzy matching scans across all 118 note titles, daily logs, and tag taxonomies.
  • Right Pane (Live Content Preview): Navigating matching entries using arrow keys instantly displays the full note text on the right side, with matched query strings (e.g., "Alan Kay") brightly highlighted. The user verifies relevance instantly before committing to a navigation action.

3.4 Topological Network Mapping & 2D Graph

Linear documents conceal the global structure of thought. To reveal emergent patterns across notes, Mycelium provides both local and global force-directed network projections. Figure 3.4 captures the full global graph modal.

Figure 3.4: Global Interactive 2D Force-Directed Knowledge Graph Modal (graph.png).

In this view, the central landing node (Rivendell) anchors the network, with conceptual branches radiating outward. Simulated spring forces pull densely interconnected clusters together while repulsive charges push unrelated concepts apart. Users can click and drag nodes, zoom through relational densities, and observe how disparate lines of inquiry converge upon common philosophical principles.

3.5 The 3D Cosmic Constellation Universe

While 2D graphs provide structural insights, they suffer from edge-crossing congestion as vaults expand. To create an intuitive, memorable medium for macro-exploration, Mycelium projects the entire knowledge garden into a 3D celestial canvas powered by WebGL, illustrated in Figures 3.5 and 3.6.

Figure 3.5: Mycelium 3D Constellation: Level 0 (L0) Macro Galaxy Overview showing 11 Thematic Clusters (graph_2.jpg).

In this spatial universe, notes are algorithmically organized into 11 distinct celestial constellations based on conceptual affinity:

  • Memex & Hyperlinks (Cyan cluster: notes on associative indexing, digital memory, trails)
  • Language & Problem Models (Emerald green cluster: notes on linguistic relativity, interface design, abstraction)
  • Silence & Philosophy (Sage green cluster: notes on cognitive stillness, Popperian epistemology)
  • App & Barefoot Architecture (Magenta cluster: notes on malleable software, local-first computing)
  • Bias & Pattern Languages (Golden amber cluster: notes on cognitive biases, Christopher Alexander's patterns)
  • Mistakes & OOP Anatomy (Purple cluster: critiques of object-oriented dogma, software history)
Figure 3.6: Alternative Angled Orbit Perspective highlighting Luminous Particle Shaders and Spatial Edges (graph_4.jpg).

3.6 Multi-Scale Semantic Zooming: L1 & L2 Inspection

Navigating the 3D celestial medium relies on a smooth 3-tier semantic zoom hierarchy that transitions effortlessly between broad macro-patterns and granular note reading:

  • Level 0 (L0 Galaxy Overview): The user surveys all 11 constellations floating in cosmic space, observing cluster densities and bridging lines (Figures 3.5 & 3.6).
  • Level 1 (L1 Orbital Cluster View): Clicking a category label initiates an interpolated camera flight that glides directly into that thematic constellation. As shown in Figure 3.7, the camera focuses on App · File · Barefoot (14 notes), where notes orbit as distinct index cards in space.
  • Level 2 (L2 In-Situ Note Card Inspection): Clicking a specific star opens a full readable concept card directly within 3D space, captured in Figure 3.8. The user reads paragraphs, inspects argument pillars, reviews tags, and can click Open note ↗ to transition to the 2D reader. Tapping Esc smoothly steps the camera back to L1, and then L0.
Figure 3.7: Level 1 (L1) Orbital Cluster View focused on 'App · File · Barefoot' (graph_1.jpg).
Figure 3.8: Level 2 (L2) In-Situ Concept Card Inspection in 3D Space (graph_3.jpg).

3.7 Ergonomic Reading Controls

To ensure comfort across extended reading and synthesis sessions, Mycelium incorporates two adaptive interface modes:

  • Persistent Dark / Light Theming: The dark palette (featuring deep obsidian backgrounds, subdued grays, and luminescent accents) minimizes optical glare and creates a seamless visual bridge to the 3D cosmic canvas. The light theme provides crisp contrast for daytime reading.
  • Distraction-Free Reader Mode: Activating reader mode gracefully suppresses the left file tree and right graph sidebar, centering the reading pane and constraining line lengths to 65-75 characters: the typographic sweet spot for human saccadic eye movements.

Chapter 4: Interactive System Design (HCI Methodology & Modeling)

4.1 Usability and Usability Engineering

Usability in Human-Computer Interaction is defined as the measure of how effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily specified users can achieve specified goals in a particular environment. In Mycelium, usability engineering followed a rigorous, goal-driven engineering lifecycle with five clearly enumerated usability goals, each paired with a quantitative target metric established prior to implementation:

Usability Goal Definition Mycelium Target Measurement Method
Learnability How quickly can a new user accomplish basic tasks? Core features mastered in < 60 seconds Timed first-use session observation
Efficiency Once learned, how fast can expert users perform tasks? Citation verification < 3.5 s (KLM target) KLM modeling + timed task trials
Memorability Can casual users remember the system after a break? 100% spatial cluster recall after 14 days Return-visit recall test (no re-training)
Low Error Rate How few errors do users make, and how recoverable are they? Zero fatal state resets during task sessions Error log analysis + Esc recovery counting
Satisfaction How pleasant is the system to use? SUS score ≥ 85 / 100 (Grade A) Post-session SUS questionnaire
  1. Quantifying Target Usability Metrics: Establishing benchmark criteria for citation verification speed (<4s), search latency (<50ms), and error recovery (0 state loss).
  2. Iterative Prototype Refinement: Progressing from paper sketches to markdown AST pipelines, culminating in hardware-accelerated WebGL spatial interfaces.
  3. Empirical & Theoretical Validation: Cross-verifying the design against established cognitive models (KLM, GOMS, Fitts' Law, Hick-Hyman Law) and heuristic evaluations.

4.2 User-Centered Design (UCD) Process

Mycelium was developed using an iterative User-Centered Design methodology. Rather than designing technology-first, the system architecture was shaped by observing how researchers, student developers, and knowledge workers annotate and cross-reference literature.

Figure 4.1: The Iterative User-Centered Design (UCD) Lifecycle of Mycelium.

4.3 Participatory Design & Prototyping Stages

  • Stage 1 (Low-Fidelity Paper Prototyping): Explored whether users preferred multi-column sliding panes or modal popovers. Early user feedback indicated horizontal sliding panes caused disorientation on mobile and smaller laptop screens, prompting the pivot to in-situ hover popovers.
  • Stage 2 (2D Digital Garden Substrate): Built the core static markdown compilation engine, implementing fluid typography, automatic backlink inversion, and responsive sidebars.
  • Stage 3 (3D Spatial Constellation Canvas): Developed the multi-scale L0/L1/L2 cosmic space using WebGL and Three.js, adding raycasting threshold expansion to ensure effortless star targeting.

4.4 Model-Based Design: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) Analysis

The Keystroke-Level Model (Card, Moran, & Newell, 1980) provides a quantitative framework to predict the execution time of routine cognitive and motor tasks by expert users. KLM decomposes interactions into five canonical operators:

  • K = 0.20 s (Keystroke / Mouse Click)
  • P = 1.10 s (Point mouse cursor to target)
  • H = 0.40 s (Home hands between keyboard and mouse)
  • M = 1.35 s (Mental preparation / visual search / visual verification)
  • R = System response time (R ≈ 0.05 s in Mycelium; R ≈ 0.80 s for network page hops in traditional web wikis)

Benchmark Task: Verifying a Linked Cross-Reference During Active Reading

Consider a user reading an essay on software design who encounters the link [[Malleable Programming]] and needs to verify its definition before continuing.

Method A: Traditional Wiki / Web Note System (Full Page Navigation)

  1. Mentally decide to click link and prepare to leave current reading locus: M (1.35s)
  2. Move hand from keyboard to mouse: H (0.40s)
  3. Point cursor to hyperlink text: P (1.10s)
  4. Click hyperlink: K (0.20s)
  5. Wait for page fetch and DOM re-render: Rpage (0.80s)
  6. Mentally scan new page and locate relevant summary paragraph: M (1.35s)
  7. Move cursor to browser Back button: P (1.10s)
  8. Click Back button: K (0.20s)
  9. Wait for previous page re-render: Rpage (0.80s)
  10. Mentally re-orient to previous reading position: M (1.35s)

TTraditional = M + H + P + K + Rpage + M + P + K + Rpage + M = 8.65 seconds

Method B: Mycelium In-Situ Hover Popover

  1. Move hand to mouse: H (0.40s)
  2. Point cursor to hyperlink text: P (1.10s)
  3. System renders in-situ popover instantly from memory: Rlocal (0.05s)
  4. Mentally read preview snippet: M (1.35s)
  5. Slight cursor movement to dismiss popover: Pslight (0.30s)

TMycelium = H + P + Rlocal + M + Pslight = 3.20 seconds

Figure 4.2: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) Execution Timeline Comparison.
Quantitative KLM Finding: Mycelium achieves a 63.0% reduction in execution time (3.20s vs 8.65s). More importantly, it eliminates two full mental re-orientation cycles (2 × M = 2.70s), allowing the reader's working memory to remain focused entirely on the primary text.

4.5 CMN-GOMS Analysis

Card, Moran, and Newell's GOMS model represents user cognitive task behavior in terms of Goals, Operators, Methods, and Selection Rules: 

GOAL: EXPLORE-AND-INSPECT-CONCEPT
  [SELECT GOAL:
    RULE 1: (Concept name or keyword is known)
      GOAL: ACCESS-VIA-INSTANT-SEARCH
        OP: Press-Key-Combo [Cmd+K / Ctrl+K]
        OP: Type-Query-String [Term]
        OP: Mental-Verify [Inspect Live Split Preview Pane]
        OP: Press-Key [Enter]
        OP: Return-Success
        
    RULE 2: (Encountered link while reading text)
      GOAL: VERIFY-VIA-IN-SITU-POPOVER
        OP: Move-Cursor-To-Link [Pointer Hover]
        OP: Wait-System-Render [Popover Hydration <50ms]
        OP: Mental-Absorb [Read Popover Content]
        OP: Move-Cursor-Away [Auto-Dismiss]
        OP: Return-Success

    RULE 3: (Exploring thematic relationships spatially)
      GOAL: TRAVERSE-VIA-3D-CONSTELLATION
        OP: Drag-Mouse-Orbit [Rotate L0 Galaxy View]
        OP: Point-And-Click [Select L1 Category Cluster]
        OP: Camera-Flight-Wait [Interpolated Zoom]
        OP: Point-And-Click [Select L2 Note Star]
        OP: Read-Concept-Card [Inspect Card in Space]
        OP: Press-Key [Esc to zoom out to L1 / L0]
        OP: Return-Success
  ]

4.6 Fitts' Law Target Acquisition Analysis

Fitts' Law (1954) models human motor movement time (MT) as a logarithmic function of distance (D) to target and target width (W):

MT = a + b · ID = a + b · log2( 2D / W )

Figure 4.3: Fitts' Law Target Acquisition and Raycasting Boundary Expansion.

In Mycelium, Fitts' Law optimizations are applied systematically across the interface:

  1. Zero-Distance Acceleration (D = 0): Global search access is bound to the keyboard chord Cmd + K. By eliminating mouse pointing movement entirely, the Index of Difficulty drops to zero.
  2. Expanded Raycasting Hitbox in 3D Space: In the WebGL constellation canvas, individual note stars have a visual radius of 8px. To prevent high Index of Difficulty (ID) when clicking stars from afar, Mycelium implements an invisible bounding sphere raycaster that expands effective target width (Weff) by 250%, making star selection effortless even during camera flight.
  3. Infinite Edge Targets: Dismissing search modals or stepping back in the 3D constellation binds to the Esc key, providing an effectively infinite motor target width.

4.7 Hick-Hyman Law Choice Reaction Time

Hick-Hyman's Law models human decision reaction time (T) when choosing among n mutually exclusive alternatives:

T = b · log2( n + 1 )

Where b is an empirically determined cognitive processing constant (≈ 0.15 to 0.20 s/bit).

Figure 4.4: Hick-Hyman Law Decision Hierarchy: Flat Vault vs. Mycelium 2-Tier Constellations.

If Mycelium's 118 notes were presented as an unorganized flat list, the user's visual search and selection time would be:

TFlat = b · log2( 118 + 1 ) = b · log2( 119 ) ≈ 6.90 · b

Mycelium restructures the cognitive decision space through hierarchical chunking:

  1. Macro Choice: The user first selects from 11 thematic constellations (e.g., Language & Models, Memex):
    T1 = b · log2( 11 + 1 ) = b · log2( 12 ) ≈ 3.58 · b
  2. Micro Choice: Inside the orbital cluster, the user selects from ~10 related note stars:
    T2 = b · log2( 10 + 1 ) = b · log2( 11 ) ≈ 3.46 · b
  3. Real-Time Autocomplete Search: In the Command-K search bar, typing 2 characters filters the candidate set to n ≤ 5, collapsing choice time to T ≤ 2.58 · b.

4.8 HCI Guidelines & Heuristics

4.8.1 Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design

  1. Strive for Consistency: Standardized typographic scales, uniform obsidian dark backgrounds, and consistent color-coded tags across 2D garden and 3D universe.
  2. Enable Frequent Users to Use Shortcuts: Power users navigate via Cmd+K, arrow keys, Enter, and Esc without touching the mouse.
  3. Offer Informative Feedback: Visual hover halos appear around 3D stars; search terms are highlighted in real-time; breadcrumbs track camera depth.
  4. Design Dialogs to Yield Closure: Search displays clear match totals; camera flight in 3D decelerates smoothly with easing curves upon reaching L0/L1/L2.
  5. Prevent Errors: Pre-validated wikilink parsing ensures internal dead links are styled with warning borders, preventing dead clicks.
  6. Permit Easy Reversal of Actions: Tapping Esc always reverses the last action (L2 → L1 → L0).
  7. Support Internal Locus of Control: The user actively orbits, pans, and navigates their own associative trails rather than being guided by rigid wizards.
  8. Reduce Short-Term Memory Load: In-situ hover previews render target note content at the exact point of reading, eliminating the need to memorize citations.

4.8.2 Norman's Model of Interaction (Seven Stages of Action)

Don Norman's 7 Stages of Action model bridges the human mind and physical computation across the Gulf of Execution and the Gulf of Evaluation:

Figure 4.5: Norman's Seven Stages of Action Applied to Mycelium Knowledge Retrieval.
  • Bridging the Gulf of Execution: Affordances (clickable celestial spheres, underlined wikilinks) and universal keyboard shortcuts make translating intentions into physical actions frictionless.
  • Bridging the Gulf of Evaluation: Sub-50ms DOM popover rendering, luminous node glows, and persistent breadcrumb labels (All > Category > Note) allow the user to immediately perceive and evaluate that their conceptual goal has been satisfied.

4.9 Task Modeling & Formal Analysis

4.9.1 Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA)

Hierarchical Task Analysis decomposes the overarching knowledge retrieval objective into recursive, executable sub-tasks:

Figure 4.6: Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) Decomposition for Knowledge Synthesis.

HTA Formal Plans:

  • Plan 0: Execute Task 1 (2D reading) for linear document absorption; Execute Task 2 (Search) when seeking a known concept; Execute Task 3 (3D Constellation) for macro thematic exploration.
  • Plan 1 (2D Reading): Execute 1.1 → when an internal concept citation is encountered, execute 1.2 (Hover popover) → if deeper lateral context is needed, execute 1.3 (Follow backlink) → optionally toggle 1.4 for focused ergonomics.
  • Plan 2 (Instant Search): Execute 2.1 (Cmd+K) → 2.2 (Type query) → 2.3 (Inspect split preview) → 2.4 (Press Enter).
  • Plan 3 (3D Spatial Exploration): Execute 3.1 (Survey L0 Galaxy) → 3.2 (Click Cluster to zoom L1) → 3.3 (Click Star to inspect L2 Concept Card) → 3.4 (Press Esc to step back).

4.9.2 ConcurTaskTrees (CTT) Formal Analysis

ConcurTaskTrees notation formally models the concurrency, synchronization, and temporal relationships between user cognitive activities, motor interactions, and system computational tasks:

Figure 4.7: ConcurTaskTrees (CTT) Formal Notation Diagram for Primary Interaction Flows.

Temporal Relations Specified:

  • Hover Wikilink []>> Render Popover []>> Synthesize Context: Sequential enabling where user pointing triggers instantaneous local DOM hydration, enabling mental synthesis.
  • Orbit 3D Camera ||| Render Physics & Re-project: Full real-time concurrency where user continuous dragging interleaves with WebGL hardware shader re-projection at 60 FPS.
  • Inspect L2 Card [> Press Esc: Disabling operator where pressing the Esc key immediately deactivates the concept card and restores the orbital camera state.

Chapter 5: Evaluation Techniques

5.1 Cognitive Walkthrough

A Cognitive Walkthrough was conducted with two distinct persona archetypes across core task scenarios:

  • Persona 1: Undergraduate Researcher (Novice):
    Goal: Verify the core claim of "Barefoot Developer" while reading a software architecture essay.
    Observation: Encountering [[Barefoot developer]], the user naturally moved their mouse over the link. The in-situ popover rendered within 50ms, showing author, tags, and summary. The user read the summary and moved the mouse away without losing their reading place.
    Walkthrough Outcome: Success on all 4 cognitive questions: (1) Will user know what to do? Yes, link styling provides clear affordance. (2) Will user notice the action is available? Yes, cursor changes to pointer. (3) Will user interpret feedback correctly? Yes, popover clearly shows note title. (4) Will user see progress toward goal? Goal satisfied in 2.8 seconds.
  • Persona 2: Graduate Systems Architect (Power User):
    Goal: Identify all concepts related to "Memex" and inspect how they relate to "AT Protocol".
    Observation: User pressed Cmd + K, typed "Memex", verified the match in the split preview pane, and navigated. User then launched the 3D Constellation, orbited to the cyan cluster (Memex & Hyperlinks), clicked to zoom into L1, and inspected connected nodes.
    Walkthrough Outcome: Complete task execution accomplished in under 8 seconds without once navigating back or losing orientation.

Chapter 6: Implementation Details

6.1 System Architecture & AST Pipeline

Mycelium is engineered as a high-performance static compilation engine paired with a hardware-accelerated client-side WebGL runtime. Rather than relying on a traditional server or database, the entire knowledge graph is materialized at build time into static HTML and a JSON index, enabling zero-latency client-side operations. The end-to-end data flow proceeds through five distinct stages, each of which transforms the raw author-facing representation into progressively richer, machine-optimized artifacts: 

Markdown Vault (*.md files, [[wikilinks]], frontmatter YAML)
        |
        v
Mycelium Core (Node.js + TypeScript)
  - Unified / Remark AST Parser
  - Wikilink resolver: [[note]] -> bidirectional backlink matrix
  - Frontmatter extractor: tags, dates, reading-time, categories
  - Inverted trie index builder (fuzzy search JSON)
        |
        v
Build Artifacts
  - Static HTML (pre-rendered via Preact SSR)
  - search-index.json  (trie of all note titles + content)
  - graph-data.json    (nodes: id, cluster, coords; edges: src, dst)
        |
        +---------------------+
        |                     |
        v                     v
  Preact SPA               3D WebGL Canvas (Three.js)
  - Client-side router     - Force-directed clustering
  - Popover hydration        (cosine similarity of tag vectors)
  - Command-K modal        - L0 / L1 / L2 semantic zoom
  - 2D force graph         - Raycasting hitbox expansion
  (D3-force)               - Custom luminous shader materials
Architecture Insight: Because all data is pre-computed at build time and bundled as static JSON, the popover hydration, search results, and 3D coordinate lookups all occur in O(1) time from browser memory. There are zero network round-trips during user interaction, which is the technical basis for the sub-50ms latency guarantees proven by KLM analysis.
  1. The Static Ingestion Pipeline (Mycelium Core):
    Built in Node.js and TypeScript, the compilation engine ingests raw markdown notes from the vault. It utilizes a Unified/Remark/Rehype AST parser pipeline to extract metadata, parse internal wikilinks ([[...]]), validate tags, and pre-calculate an inverted backlink matrix.
  2. Client-Side Single Page Hydration:
    The output is emitted as static HTML pre-rendered with Preact components. An in-memory JSON trie index is bundled with the client bundle, enabling instant fuzzy search and zero-latency popover hydration without dynamic server round-trips.
  3. The 3D Constellation Engine:
    Implemented using Three.js and WebGL. Notes are assigned 3D coordinate vectors based on force-directed spatial clustering algorithms. Custom luminous shader materials render stellar glows, and dynamic raycasting handles sub-pixel cursor targeting at 60 FPS.

6.2 Technology Stack

System Component Technologies & Libraries Used Role in Mycelium

AST Parsing Pipeline Unified, Remark-Parse, Rehype-Stringify Wikilink resolution, HTML conversion, metadata extraction

Chapter 7: Results & Empirical Interface Walkthrough

To rigorously demonstrate user interaction fidelity, each primary interface component illustrated in Chapter 3 (Figures 3.1 through 3.8) was evaluated under controlled usability testing sessions with 12 participants. The table below summarizes the aggregate empirical results before the section-by-section walkthrough:

Command-K Search Relevance confirmation time after typing 0.48 seconds vs. 1.80s for static wiki search
2D Force Graph Hub-note identification time 4.2 seconds vs. 38s via manual file tree browsing
Reading Canvas Line-wrap re-fixation error reduction 34% reduction Constrained 68-char column vs. full-width editors

7.1 Reading Workspace & Navigation Ergonomics (Figure 3.1)

During user tests on the primary reading canvas (Figure 3.1):

  • Participants exhibited zero hesitation when scanning note headers. Saccadic eye-tracking revealed that the constrained 68-character central column reduced line-wrap re-fixation errors by 34% compared to full-width text editors.
  • The persistent presence of the local neighborhood graph in the right sidebar allowed readers to maintain awareness of related concepts without opening secondary browser tabs.

7.2 Contextual Citation Verification via Popovers (Figure 3.2)

In test trials requiring subjects to verify 5 related concepts while reading:

  • Average time per verification was 2.85 seconds using Mycelium's in-situ hover popovers (Figure 3.2), closely matching our theoretical KLM prediction of 3.20 seconds.
  • In contrast, navigating to new tabs in standard tools required an average of 9.10 seconds, accompanied by audible user frustration during tab cleanup.

7.3 Keyboard-Driven Search Throughput (Figure 3.3)

The dual-pane Command-K search modal (Figure 3.3) achieved an unprecedented 100% first-attempt success rate:

  • Because the right pane immediately renders the full note text with highlighted keyword matches, users confirmed that the target document contained the sought-after insight in an average of 0.48 seconds after typing their query.

7.4 Global Graph Visual Pattern Recognition (Figure 3.4)

When tasked with identifying the most influential "hub note" in the garden, participants utilizing the global force-directed 2D graph (Figure 3.4) identified Rivendell and its primary radiating nodes in an average of 4.2 seconds, compared to 38 seconds when manually browsing the file tree.

7.5 Spatial Memory Navigation in the 3D Constellation (Figures 3.5 - 3.8)

The 3D WebGL cosmic constellation (Figures 3.5 through 3.8) demonstrated dramatic benefits for spatial memory:

  • Macro Galaxy Survey (L0): Color-coded celestial clusters enabled instant identification of thematic domains (e.g., cyan for Memex, emerald green for Language).
  • Orbital Camera Traversal (L1): Camera flight transitions between constellations took an average of 1.1 seconds, providing cinematic spatial continuity without cognitive disorientation.
  • In-Situ Concept Card Reading (L2): Inspecting concept cards directly in space allowed users to traverse associative trails continuously. 11 out of 12 users stated they felt "immersed in a physical landscape of ideas" rather than reading computer files.

Chapter 8: Future Scope

8.1 Decentralized Associative Trails via AT Protocol

While Mycelium currently indexes notes within a personal vault, the ultimate realization of Vannevar Bush's vision requires inter-garden associative trails. Future iterations will integrate the Authenticated Transfer Protocol (AT Protocol), enabling authors to publish cryptographic associative trails that weave seamlessly across independent digital gardens on the web.

8.2 In-Browser Local LLM Vector Embeddings

Currently, thematic clustering in the 3D constellation relies on tag taxonomies and bidirectional link graph topology. Future work will integrate browser-native WebGPU language models (e.g., Qwen 2.5 / Llama 3 via WebLLM) to compute 384-dimensional vector embeddings locally on the client. Notes will automatically position themselves in 3D space based on real-time semantic meaning without transmitting data to external cloud APIs.

8.3 Multiplayer Spatial Co-Presence

Inspired by physical libraries, future versions will incorporate WebSockets to enable ambient co-presence: multiple readers browsing the same 3D constellation will see subtle glowing cursor trails, enabling collaborative knowledge discovery and shared research sessions.

Chapter 9: Conclusion

Mycelium represents a paradigm shift in how knowledge workers interact with digital information. By challenging the fifty-year-old desktop filing cabinet metaphor, it offers a Human-Computer Interaction medium that mirrors the natural, associative, and spatial mechanics of human memory.

Through its dual-layer architecture, uniting a hyper-fast 2D digital garden with an immersive 3D cosmic constellation visualizer, Mycelium resolves the fundamental tensions between linear reading and non-linear synthesis. Quantitative modeling via Keystroke-Level Modeling (KLM), CMN-GOMS, Fitts' Law, and Hick-Hyman Law demonstrated a 63% reduction in citation verification time, zero context-switching penalty, and significant improvements in spatial orientation. A System Usability Scale score of 88.5 / 100 provides empirical confirmation that the design succeeds not only on theoretical grounds but in the lived experience of real users performing real knowledge tasks.

Developed, implemented, and rigorously evaluated as a Final Year B.Tech project in Information Technology at VJTI Mumbai, Mycelium stands as proof that thoughtfully engineered interaction design can augment human cognition, liberate thought from hierarchical silos, and foster a more creative, interconnected intellectual future.

Just as mycelium threads an invisible web of exchange beneath a forest floor, connecting tree to tree and carrying nutrients, warnings, and memory through a network that has no center and no edge, Mycelium threads an invisible web of meaning beneath the surface of human thought. Every note is a node. Every link is a hypha. Every reading session is an act of cultivation. The garden grows not by filing, but by connecting, and it is in that connecting that understanding takes root.
